s-5.2-requirements-techniques-outputs.title: 5.2 Collect Requirements (continued): nominal group, observation, facilitation (JAD, QFD, user stories), context diagram, prototypes, requirement classes, RTM
s-5.2-requirements-techniques-outputs.notes: Nominal group technique: structured brainstorming with voting in four steps - question posed and each person silently writes ideas; moderator records all ideas on a flip chart; each idea is discussed until understood; individuals vote privately (usually 1-5, 5 highest), possibly in several rounds, and top-scoring ideas are selected. Observation/conversation ('job shadowing'): watch people do their jobs - useful when users find it hard or are reluctant to articulate requirements; a participant observer performs the process to uncover hidden requirements. Facilitation: focused workshops bring key stakeholders together to define cross-functional requirements quickly and reconcile differences; builds trust and consensus, surfaces issues earlier; JAD (joint application design/development - software; business SMEs with the development team), QFD (quality function deployment - manufacturing; starts with the voice of the customer, sorts and prioritises needs, sets goals), user stories (short text of required functionality: role who benefits, goal, motivation/benefit), often written in requirements workshops. Context diagram: a scope model showing the business system and how actors (people, other systems) interact with it - inputs, who provides them, outputs, who receives them. Prototypes: early feedback through a model (small-scale product, 2D/3D models, mock-ups, simulations); support progressive elaboration through cycles of mock-up, experimentation, feedback and revision until requirements are complete enough for design/build; storyboarding shows sequence or navigation through images (film, advertising, instructional design, software UI). Outputs: requirements documentation - how individual requirements meet the business need; progressively detailed; before baselining requirements must be unambiguous (measurable and testable), traceable, complete, consistent and acceptable to key stakeholders. Classes: business requirements (organisation-level needs and reasons for the project); stakeholder requirements; solution requirements - functional (behaviours: actions, processes, data, interactions) and nonfunctional (environmental conditions or qualities: reliability, security, performance, safety, level of service, supportability, retention/purge); transition and readiness requirements (temporary capabilities such as data conversion and training to move from as-is to to-be); project requirements (milestone dates, contractual obligations, constraints); quality requirements (conditions to validate completion, e.g., tests, certifications, validations). Requirements traceability matrix (RTM): a grid linking product requirements from their origin to the deliverables that satisfy them; ensures each requirement adds business value; tracks requirements through the life cycle; structures product scope change management. Traces to business needs and objectives, project objectives, scope/WBS deliverables, product design, development, test strategy and scenarios, and high-level to detailed requirements. Attributes: unique ID, description, rationale, owner, source, priority, version, status (active, cancelled, deferred, added, approved, assigned, completed), status date; plus stability, complexity, acceptance criteria.

s-5.3-define-scope.title: 5.3 Define Scope: product analysis, project scope statement, charter vs scope statement
s-5.3-define-scope.notes: Develop a detailed description of the project and product; key benefit: describes product, service or result boundaries and acceptance criteria. Not every collected requirement is included - Define Scope selects the final project requirements; builds on major deliverables, assumptions and constraints from initiation; analyses risks, assumptions and constraints for completeness; can be highly iterative (in iterative life cycles a high-level vision for the whole project, detailed scope one iteration at a time). Inputs: charter (high-level description, product characteristics, approval requirements); scope management plan; documents (assumption log, requirements documentation, risk register - responses such as reducing or changing scope to avoid or mitigate a risk); EEFs; OPAs (scope statement templates, previous project files, lessons learned). Tools: expert judgment; alternatives analysis (ways to meet requirements and charter objectives); multicriteria decision analysis (decision matrix with criteria such as requirements, schedule, budget, resources to refine scope); facilitation (workshops to reach cross-functional common understanding of deliverables and boundaries); product analysis (ask questions about the product to describe its use and characteristics; translate high-level descriptions into deliverables; product breakdown, requirements analysis, systems analysis, systems engineering, value analysis, value engineering). Outputs: project scope statement - description of project scope, major deliverables, assumptions and constraints; documents entire scope (project and product); common understanding; may list explicit exclusions; enables detailed planning, guides execution, baseline for judging whether requested work is in or out of scope. Contents: product scope description (progressively elaborated), deliverables (including ancillary results like reports and documentation), acceptance criteria (conditions to be met before deliverables are accepted), project exclusions (explicitly out of scope; manages expectations and reduces scope creep). Table 5-1: charter = high-level (purpose, measurable objectives and success criteria, high-level requirements, description/boundaries/key deliverables, overall risk, summary milestones, preapproved financial resources, key stakeholders, approval requirements, exit criteria, assigned PM and authority, sponsor name and authority); scope statement = detailed (scope description, deliverables, acceptance criteria, exclusions). Document updates: assumption log, requirements documentation, RTM, stakeholder register.

s-5.4-create-wbs.title: 5.4 Create WBS: decomposition, work packages, control accounts, planning packages, 100 percent rule, WBS dictionary, scope baseline
s-5.4-create-wbs.notes: Subdivide deliverables and work into smaller, more manageable components; key benefit: a framework of what has to be delivered; once or at predefined points. The WBS is a hierarchical decomposition of the total scope of work to accomplish objectives and create deliverables; represents the approved scope statement; planned work sits in the lowest components, work packages, where activities are grouped and scheduled, estimated, monitored and controlled. 'Work' in the WBS means work products or deliverables, not activities. Inputs: scope management plan (how the WBS is created from the scope statement); documents (scope statement, requirements documentation); EEFs (industry-specific WBS standards); OPAs (WBS policies, procedures and templates, previous project files, lessons learned). Tools: expert judgment; decomposition - dividing scope and deliverables into smaller parts until the work package level, where cost and duration can be estimated and managed; level guided by needed control and project size and complexity. Steps: identify and analyse deliverables and work; structure and organise the WBS; decompose upper levels; develop and assign identification codes; verify the degree of decomposition is appropriate. Approaches: top-down, organisation-specific guidelines, WBS templates; bottom-up to group subcomponents. Forms: phases at level 2 with deliverables at level 3 (Figure 5-13, software release example); major deliverables at level 2 (Figure 5-14, aircraft system example); subcomponents from outside organisations with a seller-developed contract WBS. In agile, epics decompose into user stories. Representations: outline, organisation chart or other hierarchy. Verify that lower-level components are necessary and sufficient for their parent. Different deliverables may need different depths. More detail improves planning and control, but excessive decomposition wastes management effort and resources, lowers efficiency and makes aggregation hard. Far-future deliverables may not be decomposable yet - rolling wave planning. The WBS includes all product and project work including project management; lower levels roll up so nothing is left out and nothing extra is done - the 100 percent rule. Output: scope baseline = approved scope statement + WBS + WBS dictionary, changed only via formal change control, a plan component. Work package: lowest level, unique identifier; identifiers form a code of accounts for hierarchical summation of cost, schedule and resource information; each work package belongs to exactly one control account. Control account: management control point where scope, budget and schedule are integrated and compared to earned value; has two or more work packages. Planning package: below the control account and above the work package; known work content but no detailed schedule activities. WBS dictionary: detailed deliverable, activity and scheduling information for each WBS component - code of account identifier, description of work, assumptions and constraints, responsible organisation, milestones, associated activities, resources, cost estimates, quality requirements, acceptance criteria, technical references, agreement information (much added later by other processes). Document updates: assumption log, requirements documentation. Figures 5-12 to 5-14 are illustrative WBS examples only.

s-5.5-validate-scope.title: 5.5 Validate Scope: formal acceptance by customer or sponsor; Validate Scope vs Control Quality
s-5.5-validate-scope.notes: Formalise acceptance of completed deliverables; key benefit: objectivity in acceptance and higher probability of final acceptance by validating each deliverable; performed periodically as needed. Verified deliverables from Control Quality are reviewed with the customer or sponsor for formal acceptance, using planning outputs (requirements documentation, scope baseline) and work performance data. Validate Scope is about acceptance; Control Quality is about correctness and meeting quality requirements; Control Quality is generally performed first, though they may run in parallel. Inputs: plan (scope management plan - how acceptance is obtained; requirements management plan - how requirements are validated; scope baseline); documents (lessons learned register, quality reports, requirements documentation, RTM - how each requirement will be validated); verified deliverables (completed and checked for correctness via Control Quality); work performance data (degree of compliance, number and severity of nonconformities, validation cycles). Tools: inspection (measuring, examining, validating against requirements and acceptance criteria; also called reviews, product reviews, walkthroughs); decision making - voting when validation is by team and stakeholders. Outputs: accepted deliverables (formally signed off by customer or sponsor; documentation forwarded to Close Project or Phase); work performance information (which deliverables were accepted or not, and why); change requests (non-accepted deliverables documented with reasons; may need defect repair); document updates (lessons learned register, requirements documentation - especially results better than required or waived requirements, RTM - validation method and outcome). Data flow (Figure 5-16, verified): in from 4.3 (WPD), 8.3 (verified deliverables), plan and documents; out to 4.7 (accepted deliverables), 4.6 (change requests), 4.5 (WPI), documents.

s-5.6-control-scope.title: 5.6 Control Scope: maintaining the scope baseline, scope creep, variance and trend analysis
s-5.6-control-scope.notes: Monitor the status of project and product scope and manage changes to the scope baseline; key benefit: scope baseline maintained throughout; performed throughout. Ensures all requested changes and recommended corrective/preventive actions go through Perform Integrated Change Control; manages actual changes when they occur; integrated with other control processes. Scope creep = uncontrolled expansion of product or project scope without adjustments to time, cost and resources. Change is inevitable, so some change control process is mandatory on every project. Inputs: plan (scope, requirements, change and configuration management plans; scope baseline; performance measurement baseline); documents (lessons learned register, requirements documentation, RTM); work performance data; OPAs. Tool: data analysis (variance analysis, trend analysis). Outputs: work performance information; change requests; plan updates (scope management plan, scope baseline, schedule baseline, cost baseline, performance measurement baseline); document updates (lessons learned register, requirements documentation, RTM). Data flow (Figure 5-18, verified): WPD from 4.3; WPI to 4.5; change requests to 4.6. (Continued on PDF 206.)
